_about: Looking Glass infection knowledge base. One entry per infection name as it appears in Shadowserver reports (lower case). Fields: title, type, description, action (recommended response), confidence (high | medium | low), status (reviewed | needs-review), aliases, updated. Run manage/infections_missing.py to list infections seen in the data that have no entry yet.

android.badbox2.title: BADBOX 2.0
android.badbox2.description: Low-cost Android TV boxes, tablets and projectors shipped or updated with a backdoor that enrols them in the BADBOX 2.0 botnet. The devices are used for residential proxy services, ad fraud and click fraud.
android.badbox2.action: Identify the device behind the IP (usually an off-brand Android TV box), disconnect it and replace it. Firmware resets rarely remove the backdoor.

android.vo1d2.title: Vo1d (variant 2)
android.vo1d2.description: A newer variant of the Vo1d backdoor on Android TV boxes. Infected boxes contact the sinkholed C2 on high ports and can download and run further payloads, and the botnet is used for proxying and ad fraud.
android.vo1d2.action: Locate the Android TV box at this address, take it offline and replace it. Advise the subscriber to avoid uncertified streaming boxes.

android.vo1d.title: Vo1d
android.vo1d.description: Backdoor found on large numbers of Android TV boxes running outdated Android builds. It gives the operators remote code execution and is used to install additional malware.
android.vo1d.action: Locate and replace the TV box. Block outbound traffic from the device until it is removed.

vo1d.title: Vo1d (DNS lookups)
vo1d.description: DNS lookups for Vo1d domain-generation-algorithm (DGA) domains that are now sinkholed. The querying address hosts, or resolves for, an infected Android TV box.
vo1d.action: Treat as android.vo1d. If the IP is a DNS resolver, find the client that made the query from resolver logs.

m0yv.title: m0yv (file infector)
m0yv.description: A modular 32- and 64-bit Windows file infector, attributed to the developer of the Maze ransomware and often detected by antivirus as Expiro. It infects executable files on the machine and contacts domains generated by an algorithm (DGA), such as dlynankz.biz; those domains are sinkholed, so a host seen here is infected. Sources: NCSC Ireland (Sinkhole HTTP Events report guide) and Malpedia (win.m0yv).
m0yv.action: Treat the Windows machine as compromised. A file infector modifies programs, so reimage the machine rather than trying to clean it, check shared drives and USB media it used for infected executables, and reset credentials used on it.

ipidea.title: IPIDEA (residential proxy network)
ipidea.description: IPIDEA was one of the largest residential proxy networks. Software kits it controlled (PacketSDK, EarnSDK, CastarSDK, HexSDK), hidden in free apps, free VPNs and cheap TV boxes, turned devices into proxy exit nodes, so strangers' traffic went out through the owner's internet connection. Google found more than 550 threat groups using it in one month and disrupted it in January 2026 together with partners. Malpedia lists malware families, not proxy services, so it has no entry.
ipidea.action: Find and remove the app or device (often an Android TV box) that contains the proxy software; replace uncertified TV boxes.

netnut.title: NetNut / Popa (residential proxy network)
netnut.description: NetNut (also tracked as Popa) was a residential proxy network of at least 2 million hijacked consumer devices: software kits in apps and TV-box firmware turned them into exit nodes that NetNut rented out, and many other proxy brands resold it. Google saw 316 threat groups using it in a single week. Google and the FBI disrupted it in July 2026 and the FBI seized hundreds of its domains. Malpedia lists malware families, not proxy services, so it has no entry.
netnut.action: Find and remove the app or device that contains the proxy software (often a free app or an uncertified Android TV box).

residential-proxy.title: Residential proxy
residential-proxy.description: The device is relaying third-party traffic as a proxy exit node. Proxy software is often bundled with free apps, VPNs or pre-installed on cheap devices.
residential-proxy.action: Identify and remove the proxy software. Check the device for other malware bundled with it.

glassworm.title: GlassWorm
glassworm.description: Worm spread through compromised code-editor extensions that steals developer credentials and crypto wallets. It uses the Solana blockchain and BitTorrent DHT to find its C2, which matches the bittorrent and solana tags here.
glassworm.action: Find the developer workstation at this IP, remove malicious editor extensions, and rotate source-control, npm and cloud tokens and wallet keys.

avalanche-andromeda.title: Andromeda (Gamarue)
avalanche-andromeda.description: Andromeda, also called Gamarue, was a large modular botnet used to distribute other malware. Its infrastructure was dismantled in 2017 and its domains are sinkholed, so these are still-infected machines calling home.
avalanche-andromeda.action: Clean or reimage the Windows machine. Old Andromeda infections often spread via USB drives, so check removable media too.

avalanche.title: Avalanche network family
avalanche.description: Malware families that used the Avalanche crimeware hosting network, dismantled in 2016. Its domains remain sinkholed.
avalanche.action: Clean or reimage the infected machine.

bondat.title: Bondat (JavaScript USB worm)
bondat.description: A worm written in JavaScript that runs on Windows. It spreads through USB drives: it hides the files on the drive and puts shortcuts that look like the original folders and documents in their place, so opening one runs the worm. On the computer it starts itself at every logon, sends details of the computer (user and computer name, Windows version) to its control servers, and closes security and admin tools (antivirus, Registry Editor, Wireshark and others) to protect itself. Shadowserver sees infected computers still calling its old control servers, which are now sinkholed. Other vendors call it JS.Proslikefan or JS/Autorun.worm. Malpedia has no entry for it.
bondat.action: Run a full antivirus scan on the Windows computer, scan every USB drive that was plugged into it, and turn off Windows AutoRun.

js.worm.bondat.title: Bondat (JavaScript USB worm)
js.worm.bondat.description: A worm written in JavaScript that runs on Windows. It spreads through USB drives: it hides the files on the drive and puts shortcuts that look like the original folders and documents in their place, so opening one runs the worm. On the computer it starts itself at every logon, sends details of the computer (user and computer name, Windows version) to its control servers, and closes security and admin tools (antivirus, Registry Editor, Wireshark and others) to protect itself. Shadowserver sees infected computers still calling its old control servers, which are now sinkholed. Other vendors call it JS.Proslikefan or JS/Autorun.worm. Malpedia has no entry for it.
js.worm.bondat.action: Run a full antivirus scan on the Windows computer, scan every USB drive that was plugged into it, and turn off Windows AutoRun.

popcorntime.title: Popcorn Time (Time4Popcorn) with an abandoned updater (not malware)
popcorntime.description: An old copy of Time4Popcorn, a version of the Popcorn Time streaming app, whose built-in updater downloaded and ran programs over plain HTTP without checking them. After the makers abandoned it, anyone registering its update domains could have taken over millions of computers. Eye Security registered the domains, pushed a fix that switched the updater off and handed 15 domains to Shadowserver in March 2026. Devices still calling them have the app installed. Not malware in itself, so Malpedia does not list it.
popcorntime.action: Uninstall Popcorn Time / Time4Popcorn: it gets no security updates.

abandoned-software.title: Abandoned software
abandoned-software.description: Software whose vendor no longer controls its update or telemetry domains, which are now sinkholed.

android.midnight-mimosa.title: Midnight Mimosa (preinstalled Android malware)
android.midnight-mimosa.type: Android malware (preinstalled; ad fraud and residential proxy)
android.midnight-mimosa.description: Malware that comes preinstalled on some cheap Android phones (often MediaTek-based models): a hidden system app that cannot be uninstalled normally. It quietly downloads and installs other apps and runs advertising and click fraud in the background; some of its add-ons turn the phone into a residential proxy, so strangers send their internet traffic through the owner's connection. Bitdefender Labs found it on thousands of devices in more than 150 countries over about two years (report published October 2026). Shadowserver sees infected phones contacting its sinkholed servers. Malpedia has no entry for it yet.
android.midnight-mimosa.action: Identify the Android device, remove recently installed or unknown apps, or factory reset it.

amadey.title: Amadey
amadey.description: Amadey is a Windows bot used to steal data and download further malware such as infostealers and ransomware. These events come from Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit sinkhole.
amadey.action: Isolate and reimage the machine, and reset all passwords and session tokens that were used on it.

ranbyus.title: Ranbyus
ranbyus.description: Windows banking trojan that steals online-banking credentials. It uses a domain generation algorithm (DGA), and its domains are sinkholed.
ranbyus.action: Reimage the machine and have the user change banking passwords from a clean device.

avalanche-ranbyus.title: Ranbyus (Avalanche)
avalanche-ranbyus.description: Ranbyus banking trojan that used the Avalanche hosting network. Its domains are sinkholed.
avalanche-ranbyus.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

ngioweb.title: Ngioweb
ngioweb.description: Malware for Linux servers, routers and IoT devices that turns them into proxies, sold through residential proxy services. It finds its C2 using a domain generation algorithm.
ngioweb.action: Find the router, NAS or Linux device at this IP, update its firmware, change its admin passwords and close exposed management ports.

nymaim.title: Nymaim
nymaim.description: Windows downloader that installs other malware, historically ransomware and banking trojans. It uses a domain generation algorithm (DGA).
nymaim.action: Reimage the machine and check for secondary infections.

avalanche-nymaim.title: Nymaim (Avalanche)
avalanche-nymaim.description: Nymaim downloader that used the Avalanche hosting network.
avalanche-nymaim.action: Reimage the machine and check for secondary infections.

smokeloader.title: SmokeLoader
smokeloader.description: Long-running modular Windows loader used to deliver infostealers, ransomware and other payloads. It was targeted by the international Operation Endgame takedowns.
smokeloader.action: Isolate and reimage the machine. Assume credentials on it were stolen.

911-socks5-proxy.title: 911 S5 (residential proxy botnet)
911-socks5-proxy.description: 911 S5 was a criminal 'residential proxy' service: free VPN apps such as MaskVPN, DewVPN, PaladinVPN, ProxyGate, ShieldVPN and ShineVPN secretly turned the computers they were installed on into proxies, and criminals rented those home internet connections to hide fraud, cyber-attacks and other crimes. About 19 million addresses in more than 190 countries were affected. The FBI and partners took it down in May 2024 and arrested its administrator. The device is still calling 911 S5's seized servers. Malpedia has no entry for it.
911-socks5-proxy.action: Uninstall the VPN apps named above (the FBI's page explains how), then run an antivirus scan.

pykspa.title: Pykspa
pykspa.description: Old Windows worm that spread through Skype messages and uses a domain generation algorithm for C2.

kovter.title: Kovter
kovter.description: Largely fileless Windows malware used for ad and click fraud. It was part of the 3ve ad-fraud operation taken down in 2018, which matches the 3ve tag.
kovter.action: Reimage the machine. Kovter hides in the registry, so file-only scans can miss it.

boaxxe.title: Boaxxe
boaxxe.description: Windows malware used for ad fraud as part of the 3ve operation taken down in 2018.

3ve.title: 3ve ad-fraud operation
3ve.description: Large ad-fraud operation built on the Kovter and Boaxxe botnets, dismantled in 2018.

vipersoftx.title: ViperSoftX
vipersoftx.description: Windows stealer spread through cracked software and torrents. It targets cryptocurrency wallets and browser data and can install a malicious browser extension.
vipersoftx.action: Reimage the machine, move crypto funds to new wallets created on a clean device, and reset passwords.

likely-rat-adwind.title: Adwind RAT (likely)
likely-rat-adwind.description: Traffic consistent with Adwind (jRAT), a Java-based cross-platform remote access trojan sold as a service. Shadowserver marks this identification as likely rather than confirmed.
likely-rat-adwind.action: Treat the host as compromised: isolate it, check for Java-based malware, and reset credentials.

pseudomanuscrypt.title: PseudoManuscrypt
pseudomanuscrypt.description: Spyware for Windows, spread through fake installers for pirated software and key generators (and by the Glupteba botnet). It records keystrokes and the clipboard, steals VPN connection details, can record from the microphone and takes screenshots. Kaspersky counted more than 35,000 infected computers in 195 countries in 2021, at least 7% of them industrial-control (ICS) computers. It is named after Lazarus' Manuscrypt malware, which it resembles.
pseudomanuscrypt.action: Isolate and reimage the machine. If it is on an industrial or OT network, escalate.

lumma-stealer-beacon.title: Lumma Stealer (beacon)
lumma-stealer-beacon.description: An infected machine checking in with Lumma Stealer infrastructure seized by Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit. Lumma steals browser passwords, cookies, session tokens and crypto wallets.
lumma-stealer-beacon.action: Isolate and reimage the machine. Revoke the user's sessions and tokens and reset all passwords from a clean device.

lumma-stealer-download.title: Lumma Stealer (download)
lumma-stealer-download.description: The machine tried to download Lumma Stealer components from seized infrastructure, so an infection was in progress or already present.
lumma-stealer-download.action: Same as Lumma beacon: reimage, revoke sessions and reset passwords.

matsnu.title: Matsnu
matsnu.description: Windows backdoor with ransomware features. It uses a dictionary-based domain generation algorithm, so its domains look like joined English words.

avalanche-matsnu.title: Matsnu (Avalanche)
avalanche-matsnu.description: Matsnu backdoor that used the Avalanche hosting network.

adload.title: AdLoad (macOS adware)
adload.description: AdLoad is adware for Apple Mac computers. It hijacks the web browser: it sends the user's web traffic through the attackers' own proxy to change search results and inject advertising. Newer versions also turn the Mac into a proxy exit node, so other people's internet traffic goes out through the owner's connection. It keeps changing to slip past Apple's built-in XProtect protection (SentinelOne, 2021 and 2024; AT&T Alien Labs, 2023). Malpedia has no entry for it.
adload.action: Run an up-to-date anti-malware scan on the Mac, remove unknown apps, launch agents and browser extensions.

qsnatch.title: QSnatch
qsnatch.description: Malware that infects QNAP network-attached storage devices, steals credentials and blocks firmware updates. National cyber agencies issued alerts about it in 2020.
qsnatch.action: Find the QNAP NAS at this IP, factory reset it, update its firmware, change all passwords, and remove it from direct internet exposure.

necurs.title: Necurs
necurs.description: Once one of the largest spam botnets, used to distribute Dridex and Locky. Microsoft and partners disrupted it in 2020, and its DGA domains are sinkholed.

avalanche-goznym.title: GozNym (banking trojan, Avalanche network)
avalanche-goznym.description: GozNym is a banking trojan for Windows built by combining two older ones, Nymaim and Gozi. It steals online-banking log-ins to empty victims' accounts; its operators stole an estimated USD 100 million from more than 41,000 victims. It was hosted on the Avalanche criminal network; the network was taken down in 2016 and the gang charged in May 2019 (Europol, Eurojust, US Department of Justice). The device is still calling GozNym's sinkholed domains. Malpedia lists the two parts separately (win.nymaim, win.gozi), not GozNym itself.
avalanche-goznym.action: Reinstall the computer, then change online-banking passwords from a clean device and tell the bank.

worm.phorpiex.title: Phorpiex (Trik)
worm.phorpiex.description: Long-running Windows worm and botnet used for sextortion spam, ransomware delivery and cryptocurrency clipboard hijacking.
worm.phorpiex.action: Reimage the machine and check USB drives. Warn the user about clipboard address swapping if they use crypto.

cryptolocker.title: CryptoLocker
cryptolocker.description: Early file-encrypting ransomware from 2013 whose infrastructure was taken down with Gameover Zeus in 2014. Queries for its DGA domains point to old or dormant infections.
cryptolocker.action: Reimage the machine. Dormant ransomware should never be left in place.

non-authoritative-whois.title: Out-of-date .mobi WHOIS server (not malware)
non-authoritative-whois.description: Software on this machine still asks the old WHOIS server of the .mobi domain (whois.dotmobiregistry.net), whose domain expired. In 2024 researchers at watchTowr registered it and showed that anyone holding it could send false answers, for example to trick certificate authorities. It was handed to Shadowserver, which forwards the questions to the right server and reports who still uses the old one. Not malware, so Malpedia does not list it.
non-authoritative-whois.action: Update the software (or its WHOIS settings) to use whois.nic.mobi.

avalanche-panda-banker.title: Panda Banker
avalanche-panda-banker.description: Zeus-based banking trojan that injects into browsers to steal financial credentials.
avalanche-panda-banker.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

avalanche-tiny-banker.title: Tinba (Tiny Banker)
avalanche-tiny-banker.description: Very small banking trojan that injects into browsers to steal online-banking credentials.
avalanche-tiny-banker.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

avalanche-unknown.title: Avalanche network (malware family not identified)
avalanche-unknown.description: Avalanche was a criminal hosting network that hid the servers of more than 20 malware families (banking trojans, ransomware, spam bots) behind constantly changing infected computers ('fast flux'). Police in many countries took it down in December 2016, and Shadowserver took over its more than 800,000 domains (a 'sinkhole'). Computers still infected keep calling those domains, which is how they are found. The device looked up Avalanche domains that cannot be tied to one malware family. Malpedia lists families, not networks, so it has no entry.
avalanche-unknown.action: Treat the computer as infected: run a full antivirus scan and, if anything is found, reinstall it.

avalanche-generic.title: Avalanche network (malware family not identified)
avalanche-generic.description: Avalanche was a criminal hosting network that hid the servers of more than 20 malware families (banking trojans, ransomware, spam bots) behind constantly changing infected computers ('fast flux'). Police in many countries took it down in December 2016, and Shadowserver took over its more than 800,000 domains (a 'sinkhole'). Computers still infected keep calling those domains, which is how they are found. For this record Shadowserver could not tell which of the Avalanche malware families is on the device, so it is reported under the general Avalanche label. Malpedia lists families, not networks, so it has no entry.
avalanche-generic.action: Treat the computer as infected: run a full antivirus scan and, if anything is found, reinstall it.

locky.title: Locky
locky.description: Ransomware widely spread in 2016 through Necurs spam. Lookups of its DGA domains indicate a dormant or failed infection.

sality.title: Sality
sality.description: Old polymorphic Windows virus that infects executable files and forms a peer-to-peer botnet.
sality.action: Reimage the machine. Executables on shared drives it touched may also be infected.

sality-p2p.title: Sality (P2P)
sality-p2p.description: Sality-infected machine talking to the botnet's peer-to-peer network.
sality-p2p.action: Reimage the machine and check shared drives for infected executables.

modpack.title: ModPack (Misfox)
modpack.description: The Windows malware family Malpedia lists as Misfox, also known as MixFox, Dromedan and ModPack. Its domain (seen here as a .ru domain) is sinkholed, so a host seen here is infected. Malpedia holds no further description of its behaviour. Source: Malpedia (win.misfox).
modpack.action: Treat the Windows machine as compromised: scan it with up-to-date endpoint protection or reimage it, and reset credentials used on it.

jackskid.title: Jackskid (RCtea)
jackskid.description: A Mirai-derived DDoS botnet for Linux and IoT devices, first documented in November 2025 and also tracked as RCtea. Later versions also target Android TV boxes with exposed debugging (ADB) and are used as residential proxies. Its infrastructure was disrupted by law enforcement in March 2026, and its domains (seen here as richylam.org) are sinkholed, so a host seen here is infected. Source: Malpedia (elf.jackskid).
jackskid.action: Identify the device behind the IP (usually a router, camera, DVR or Android TV box), reboot it and update its firmware, change default passwords, and close remote access ports such as Telnet and ADB (5555) from the internet. Replace devices that no longer receive updates.

dragon-boss.title: Dragon Boss Solutions adware (Chromstera browser)
dragon-boss.description: Adware from a company called Dragon Boss Solutions, installed as fake web browsers such as Chromstera, Chromnius and Artificius. It takes over the browser to redirect searches for profit. In 2026 Huntress found that its update mechanism also pushed a script that switched off antivirus protection on more than 23,000 computers in 124 countries, and that the update channel could have been taken over by anyone. Shadowserver now holds one of its domains. Malpedia has no entry for it.
dragon-boss.action: Uninstall Chromstera / Chromnius / Artificius and any Dragon Boss software, check that antivirus is switched on again, and run a full scan.

giftedvisitor.title: GIFTEDVISITOR
giftedvisitor.description: Malware linked to the UTA0178 intrusions into Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances reported by Volexity, which matches the tags here. A hit suggests the address hosts or reaches a compromised VPN appliance.
giftedvisitor.action: High priority: check any Ivanti Connect Secure appliance at this address with the vendor integrity tool, patch it and rotate all credentials it handles. Escalate as a possible targeted intrusion.

avalanche-xswkit.title: xswkit (Avalanche)
avalanche-xswkit.type: Malware distributed by the Avalanche crimeware network
avalanche-xswkit.description: One of the malware families spread through the Avalanche network, a crimeware infrastructure of about twenty botnets used for spam, phishing, ransomware and banking trojans. Avalanche was taken down on 30 November 2016 by German authorities with law enforcement in 30 countries, and more than 800,000 of its domains were sinkholed. A device still contacting those domains carries a family Avalanche distributed, usually on Windows (sometimes Android). Detail on xswkit itself is limited. Source: NCSC Ireland (Sinkhole HTTP Events report guide).
avalanche-xswkit.action: Treat the machine as infected: scan it with up-to-date endpoint protection or reimage it, and reset credentials used on it (Avalanche families often stole banking and login details).

cobaltstrike.title: Cobalt Strike
cobaltstrike.description: Commercial penetration-testing framework widely abused by ransomware gangs and state-linked actors. The nobelium tag points to a domain tied to that actor's past operations.
cobaltstrike.action: High priority: unless this is a sanctioned penetration test, treat it as an active intrusion. Isolate the host and investigate lateral movement.

orchard.title: Orchard
orchard.description: Botnet that generates its C2 domains from Bitcoin blockchain information, so they cannot be predicted in advance.

avalanche-teslacrypt.title: TeslaCrypt
avalanche-teslacrypt.description: Ransomware active in 2015 and 2016. Its operators released the master decryption key when they shut it down.
avalanche-teslacrypt.action: Reimage the machine. Files encrypted by TeslaCrypt can be decrypted with the public tools.

dltminer.title: DLTMiner
dltminer.description: Mining malware spread through vulnerable Microsoft Exchange servers, which matches the msexchange tag, and through weak SMB credentials.
dltminer.action: Check any Exchange server at this address for web shells and missing patches, then remove the miner.

avalanche-urlzone.title: URLZone (Bebloh)
avalanche-urlzone.description: Banking trojan, also called Bebloh or Shiotob, distributed by spam and historically focused on European banks.
avalanche-urlzone.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

avalanche-corebot.title: CoreBot
avalanche-corebot.description: Modular Windows trojan that steals credentials and can load banking modules. It used the Avalanche network's DGA domains.
avalanche-corebot.action: Reimage the machine and reset passwords from a clean device.

avalanche-tinba.title: Tinba (Avalanche)
avalanche-tinba.description: Tinba (Tiny Banker) banking trojan that used the Avalanche hosting network.
avalanche-tinba.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

tinba.title: Tinba (Tiny Banker)
tinba.description: Very small banking trojan that injects into browsers to steal online-banking credentials. It uses a domain generation algorithm (DGA).
tinba.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

virut.title: Virut
virut.description: Old polymorphic virus that infects executables and HTML files and joins an IRC-controlled botnet. Its domains were taken over and sinkholed in 2013.
virut.action: Reimage the machine. Infected executables on shared drives can re-infect other machines.

avalanche-vmzeus.title: VM Zeus
avalanche-vmzeus.description: Variant of the Zeus banking trojan with anti-analysis features. It used the Avalanche hosting network.
avalanche-vmzeus.action: Reimage the machine and change banking passwords from a clean device.

socks5systemz.title: Socks5Systemz
socks5systemz.description: Windows proxy botnet, often dropped by malware loaders, that sells access to infected machines as SOCKS5 proxies.
socks5systemz.action: Reimage the machine. The loader that installed it may have dropped other malware too.

avalanche-rovnix.title: Rovnix
avalanche-rovnix.description: Banking trojan with a bootkit component that hides in the boot area of the disk, so it survives ordinary cleanup.
avalanche-rovnix.action: Reimage the machine, including the boot sector, and change banking passwords from a clean device.

sharkbot.title: SharkBot
sharkbot.description: Android banking trojan spread through fake apps. It overlays banking apps and can make fraudulent transfers automatically.
sharkbot.action: Identify the phone, remove the malicious app or factory reset it, and have the user contact their bank.

enfal-apt.title: Enfal
enfal-apt.description: Backdoor, also called Lurid, used in long-running espionage campaigns against government and other organisations.
enfal-apt.action: High priority: treat as a possible targeted intrusion. Isolate the host and escalate.

xcsset.title: XCSSET
xcsset.description: macOS malware that spreads through infected Xcode projects and steals browser data, cookies and app data.
xcsset.action: Identify the Mac (often a developer machine), remove infected Xcode projects, reinstall macOS and rotate credentials.

infy.title: Infy (Prince of Persia)
infy.description: Long-running espionage malware family attributed to an Iran-linked actor, also called Prince of Persia. It targets specific individuals and organisations.
infy.action: High priority: treat as a possible targeted intrusion. Isolate the host and escalate.

event4_sinkhole_dns.title: DNS look-up of a sinkholed domain (resolver, not the infected device)
event4_sinkhole_dns.description: Comes from Shadowserver's Sinkhole DNS Events report. The address is a DNS resolver (for example an ISP's or a company's DNS server) that asked for a domain Shadowserver holds, on behalf of some device behind it. The resolver is not infected itself: the infected device is one of its users, and the report does not say which malware it was. Malpedia lists malware families, so there is nothing to match.
event4_sinkhole_dns.action: Check the resolver's own query logs for who asked for the domain, and scan that device.

http-scan.title: HTTP scanning
http-scan.description: This host probed a web honeypot for vulnerable paths and admin pages, a sign of automated exploitation tooling or an infected device.
http-scan.action: Find out why the host is scanning. Usually it is a compromised server or router, or a bot.

ssh-brute-force.title: SSH brute force
ssh-brute-force.description: This host repeatedly tried to log in to an SSH honeypot with guessed usernames and passwords. The detail view shows the credentials it tried.
ssh-brute-force.action: The source is likely a compromised server or IoT device. Find it, change its passwords and disable password logins for SSH.

telnet-brute-force.title: Telnet brute force
telnet-brute-force.description: This host repeatedly tried to log in to a Telnet honeypot, typical of IoT botnets such as Mirai spreading to new devices.
telnet-brute-force.action: Find the IoT device or router, change default passwords, update firmware and disable Telnet.

smb-scan.title: SMB scanning
smb-scan.description: This host probed a honeypot over SMB (port 445), a technique used by worms and ransomware for spreading.
smb-scan.action: Find the scanning host and check it for worm or ransomware activity.

rdp-scan.title: RDP scanning
rdp-scan.description: This host probed a honeypot for Remote Desktop, often a precursor to credential attacks.
rdp-scan.action: Find the scanning host and check it for compromise.

adb-scan.title: ADB scanning
adb-scan.description: This host probed a honeypot for the Android Debug Bridge, used by botnets to infect exposed Android devices.
adb-scan.action: Find the host. It is often an infected Android device or TV box.

ddos-participant.title: DDoS participant
ddos-participant.description: This host took part in a denial-of-service attack observed by a DDoS protection provider. The detail view shows the attack type and duration.
ddos-participant.action: Find the device, which is usually an infected IoT device or server, and clean it.

ddos-amplification.title: DDoS amplification
ddos-amplification.description: This host answered spoofed requests and sent amplified traffic toward a victim, typically through open DNS, NTP or similar UDP services.
ddos-amplification.action: Close or rate-limit the open UDP service on the host.

ddos-target.title: DDoS target
ddos-target.description: A local network was the target of a DDoS attack command observed by a honeypot.
ddos-target.action: Inform the owner of the targeted network and review DDoS protection.

mirai.title: Mirai
mirai.description: IoT botnet family that spreads by brute-forcing Telnet and exploiting routers and cameras. It is used for DDoS attacks.
mirai.action: Find the IoT device, change default credentials, update firmware and disable Telnet.

ip-spoofer.title: IP spoofing possible
ip-spoofer.description: The network allowed packets with forged source addresses to leave it (failed BCP38 filtering), which enables reflection DDoS attacks.
ip-spoofer.action: Apply ingress and egress source-address filtering (BCP38) on the network edge.

executed-clearfake-payload.title: ClearFake payload executed
executed-clearfake-payload.description: A user ran a payload from the ClearFake fake-browser-update and ClickFix campaign, which usually installs an infostealer or loader.
executed-clearfake-payload.action: High priority: isolate and reimage the machine, then reset the user's passwords and sessions.

socks-escort.title: SocksEscort (proxy service on AVrecon-infected routers)
socks-escort.description: SocksEscort was a criminal proxy service that sold access to home and small-office routers and other edge devices infected with the AVrecon Linux malware (about 1,200 models from Cisco, D-Link, Hikvision, MikroTik, Netgear, TP-Link, Zyxel and others): about 369,000 addresses in 163 countries. US and European police took it down in March 2026 ('Operation Lightning'), with help from Lumen Black Lotus Labs and Shadowserver. The device, usually a router, is still calling its seized servers. Malpedia has no entry under this name.
socks-escort.action: Reset the router to factory settings, install the latest firmware (or replace it if no longer supported) and change its admin password.

cryptodns-resolver.title: Crypto DNS resolver (blockchain domain names, e.g. Namecoin .bit)
cryptodns-resolver.description: The device used a 'crypto DNS' resolver: a server that looks up domain names kept on a blockchain, such as Namecoin's .bit, instead of normal internet domains. Such names cannot be suspended by a registrar, so criminals used them to hide the control servers of malware (Smoke Loader, Necurs, Chthonic, Shifu, TinyNuke and others); infected computers asked public crypto-DNS resolvers for them. The resolver this device asked is now held by Shadowserver. It means either malware on the device looking for its servers, or software that was deliberately set up to use crypto DNS. A changed DNS setting on a computer is itself a warning sign (Carnegie Mellon SEI, 2018). Not a malware family, so Malpedia does not list it.
cryptodns-resolver.action: Check the device's DNS settings and what changed them; run a full antivirus scan.
